incidente.resumo: During the AWS us-east-1 outage on October 20, 2025, AWS-hosted third parties incident.io depends on failed, impacting on-call notifications (a telecom provider outage plus client retries backed up a shared notification queue), SAML authentication, Scribe and briefly Status Pages. A deployment pipeline that depended on a Docker Hub base image, Postgres dead tuples and a rate-limiter change that applied limits to only 10 organisations hampered the response; notifications stabilised after deployment fixes were applied once Docker Hub partially recovered.

descricao.texto: At 07:21 UTC an on-call engineer was paged due to high error rates sending SMS messages and making phone calls; the telecom provider then confirmed the impact on its status page.
trechos: At 07:21 UTC, one of our on-call engineers was paged due to high error rates sending SMS messages and making phone calls. Shortly after, our provider confirmed the impact via their own status page.

gatilho.texto: AWS had a major outage in its us-east-1 region from 07:11 to 10:53 UTC on October 20, 2025.
trechos: One of these happened on Monday, October 20, when AWS had a widely covered major outage in their us-east-1 region, from 07:11 to 10:53 UTC.

descricao.texto: Although the platform is hosted in multiple Google Cloud regions, it depends on third parties that are hosted in AWS or have AWS dependencies (a transcription provider and a SAML authentication provider hosted in AWS), and the telecom provider had an outage from 07:20 to 09:26 UTC; as a result the AWS outage impacted on-call notifications, SAML authentication and Scribe.
trechos: We’re hosted in multiple regions of Google Cloud and so the majority of our product was unaffected by the outage. However, we do depend on third parties for some aspects of our platform, who themselves are hosted in AWS, or have their own dependencies that are.
As a result, the outage impacted several of our key services, including on-call notifications, SAML authentication, and Scribe, our incident note taker.
Our transcription provider was hosted in AWS and as a result, unavailable between 07:34 to 10:07 UTC and then again between 12:40 to 17:37 UTC.
Our SAML authentication provider was also hosted in AWS and significantly degraded between 07:17 and 09:28 UTC.
Our telecom provider had an outage between 07:20 and 09:26 UTC, which delayed on-call notification delivery via SMS messages and phone calls.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Failing telecom requests combined with client retry mechanisms made notification jobs take up to 30s (60x their normal duration) under up to 30x normal load, so the notification queue grew; because senders shared capacity between notification queues, Email, Slack, APNS and Android push notifications were also impacted.
trechos: It was immediately clear the failing telecom requests, combined with our client retry mechanisms were resulting in notification jobs taking up to 30s to process.

At 60x their normal duration, combined with up to 30x normal load, this was causing the notification queue to gradually increase in length. This impacted more than just SMS and phone notifications as the senders were sharing capacity between notification queues.

Crucially, unexpected dependencies impacted several of our standard incident response options (discussed below) as well as other notification methods including Email, Slack, APNS (Apple Push Notifications) and push notifications on Android - something which shouldn’t have been possible.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The deployment pipeline failed because the build's base image golang:1.24.9-alpine resolved to a Docker registry image and Docker runs its registry on AWS; Buildkite containers also needed Docker registry images to start, and the daemon made failing HEAD requests to Docker even for cached images, so code fixes could not be deployed until Docker Hub partially recovered at 09:45 UTC.
trechos: Sadly, this was not the case. Our deployment pipeline failed, with the following error:
golang:1.24.9-alpine:
Crucially, this resolved to a Docker registry image, and Docker runs their registry on AWS.
This deployment change triggered a restart of our Buildkite containers, which couldn't start: they also needed access to Docker registry images.
However, the daemon still made (failing) HEAD requests to Docker, even for cached images.
Ultimately, it wasn’t until Docker Hub partially recovered at 09:45 UTC that we were able to capture a base image and get our deployment pipeline working again.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The Postgres index used to find the next available escalation filled with dead tuples, forcing scans of old rows; escalation acquisition grew to almost ~50% of worker capacity, so adding escalation workers decreased throughput and increased pressure on the database.
trechos: The red shows the time spent by our workers acquiring escalations from our queue, where acquisition had began to represent a substantial amount of the total worker capacity.
During the incident it had crept-up to almost ~50% of available worker capacity.

The index Postgres uses to find the next available escalation to work was filling with dead tuples, and as tuple visibility isn’t present in Postgres indexes, it was forced to scan old rows before finding the next escalation candidate.
Increasing our capacity to work escalations did not result in a net increase in escalation throughput (in fact, it decreased throughput)
Acquisition had now become very expensive, so adding workers also increased pressure on our database

fatores_contribuintes.texto: A recent usability improvement to the custom rate-limiter (traffic) resulted in limits being applied only to the top 10 organisations by traffic volume, so setting phone and SMS limits to 0 applied only to a subset, and the change could not be reverted while the deployment pipeline was down.
trechos: We set the limits for phone and SMS notifications to 0 and waited. Soon after, the CLI had successfully applied the limits, but only to a subset.
On investigation, we found that a recent usability improvement resulted in limits only being applied to the top 10 organisations by traffic volumes.

This was unexpected and unfortunately, the deployment pipeline being down as outlined above, meant we were unable to revert the change until our deployment pipeline was back up (at which point, the issue was immediately resolved).

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Authentication relies on a single SAML provider; the fallback of SSO via Slack and Microsoft Teams also became intermittent as Slack's platform entered a degraded state.
trechos: Whilst we rely on a single SAML provider, we still support multiple authentication methods, so many users were still able to log in using SSO via Slack and Microsoft Teams initially.
Unfortunately, as the outage progressed, Slack’s platform also entered a degraded state, causing intermittent login failures.

passos.texto: Within 10 minutes of the first page, prepared two PRs: one to temporarily no-op SMS and phone notifications and one to split the queues so different notification types run on isolated worker pools; deployment failed at first.
trechos: Within 10 minutes of the first page, we had two PRs ready to merge, one that would temporarily no-op SMS and phone notifications during the outage, and another that would split the queues to ensure different notification types were handled by isolated worker pools.
Sadly, this was not the case. Our deployment pipeline failed, with the following error:

passos.texto: Tried to unblock the deployment pipeline: reconfigured the container build to fetch the base image from mirror.gcr.io (the restarted Buildkite containers could not start), and disabled auto-scaling and purged newer Kubernetes VMs hoping to use local image caches (the daemon still made failing HEAD requests to Docker).
trechos: First we reconfigured our container build to use mirror.gcr.io so we could fetch the base image from Google’s Docker mirror.
This deployment change triggered a restart of our Buildkite containers, which couldn't start: they also needed access to Docker registry images.
We tried disabling auto-scaling and purged newer VMs from our Kubernetes cluster.
However, the daemon still made (failing) HEAD requests to Docker, even for cached images.

passos.texto: Added replicas to the escalation and notification Kubernetes deployment at 07:52 and 08:04 UTC; because of dead tuples in the Postgres escalation index, this did not increase escalation throughput.
trechos: Given its criticality, we have a Kubernetes deployment tasked exclusively with running our escalation and notification system.
You can see us adding replicas at 07:52 and 08:04 UTC, but due to the large amount of activity from the AWS outage, this system was already under atypical load.
Increasing our capacity to work escalations did not result in a net increase in escalation throughput (in fact, it decreased throughput)

passos.texto: Set the traffic rate-limiter limits for phone and SMS notifications to 0, which applied only to a subset of organisations.
trechos: We set the limits for phone and SMS notifications to 0 and waited. Soon after, the CLI had successfully applied the limits, but only to a subset.

passos.texto: After Docker Hub partially recovered at 09:45 UTC, captured a base image and got the deployment pipeline working; the earlier deployment fixes were applied and notifications became stable, and the rate-limiter change was reverted, resolving that issue.
trechos: Ultimately, it wasn’t until Docker Hub partially recovered at 09:45 UTC that we were able to capture a base image and get our deployment pipeline working again.
Thankfully by this time, the earlier deployment fixes had been applied and so notifications had been stable for a while (albeit more expensive to process than they should be).

This was unexpected and unfortunately, the deployment pipeline being down as outlined above, meant we were unable to revert the change until our deployment pipeline was back up (at which point, the issue was immediately resolved).

passos.texto: Decreased Postgres autovacuum thresholds and changed the escalation acquisition logic to avoid churn; these were released to production late in the incident.
trechos: We managed to combat acquisition cost by decreasing our autovacuum thresholds and changing our escalation acquisition logic to avoid this type of churn.
These fixes mean we won’t be affected by this problem again, but the deployment pipeline issues meant we only released them to production late in the incident.

passos.texto: For Scribe, reworked the implementation with the upstream provider to dynamically transition workloads to a different AWS region; by 17:36 UTC it was in place and Scribe was joining calls consistently.
trechos: We worked closely with our upstream provider and were able to rework our implementation to dynamically transition workloads to a different AWS region in case of failure.
By 17:36 UTC, it was in place and Scribe was joining calls consistently - we’re now more resilient to similar outages in future.

acoes.texto: Already done: removed the implicit dependency on Docker Hub, consolidated all direct and transitive build and deployment dependencies, and reworked the deployment pipeline to be entirely self-sufficient within GCP.
trechos: We've already removed this dependency and reworked our deployment pipeline to be entirely self sufficient and based within GCP.
Removed the implicit dependency on Docker Hub and consolidated all direct and transitive build and deployment dependencies

acoes.texto: Already done: added full region switching capabilities via the third-party transcription provider to react better to regional failures. Planned: make failure modes much clearer.
trechos: We added full region switching capabilities via the third-party provider to allow us to react better to regional failures. We'll also be looking at making failure modes much clearer.

acoes.texto: In progress: ensuring multiple telecom providers in different clouds and regions, which was already on the roadmap and will get more focus in the short term.
trechos: On telecoms redundancy
Ensuring we have multiple providers in different clouds and regions was already on our roadmap and is currently being actively worked on.
The timing here was therefore particularly painful, but we'll ensure this gets even more focus in the short term, and is rolled out as soon as possible.

acoes.texto: Already done: optimised escalation acquisition to reduce table churn (lowering dead tuples), put more sensitive alerting thresholds in place, and applied aggressive autovacuum settings to prevent dead tuple build-up.
trechos: We optimised escalation acquisition to reduce table churn (lowering dead tuples) and put more sensitive alerting thresholds in place
We applied aggressive autovacuum settings to prevent dead tuple build-up

acoes.texto: Already done: split worker capacity for notification sending from the escalation worker system and segmented all notification senders by provider.
trechos: We split worker capacity for notification sending from the escalation worker system and segmented all notification senders by provider

acoes.texto: Already done: reviewed capacity posture and pre-emptively scaled several deployments to handle burst traffic at the scale of an AWS us-east-1 outage. In progress: further review of the response and systems over the next few weeks.
trechos: We reviewed capacity posture and have pre-emptively scaled several of our deployments to better handle burst traffic for "AWS us-east-1 outage" scale
In addition to the above, we're continue to review our response and systems in more depth and make further improvements over the next few weeks.

perguntas_em_aberto: The authors are still working with their Status Pages infrastructure provider to understand why the europe-west3 and australia-southeast1 regions were so heavily affected compared with others.

observacoes: The document gives separate windows per service and no single impact start and end: telecom provider outage 07:20-09:26 UTC, SAML provider degraded 07:17-09:28 UTC, Scribe unavailable 07:34-10:07 and 12:40-17:37 UTC, Status Pages errors (about 4% of traffic) 07:54-08:19 UTC, AWS us-east-1 outage 07:11-10:53 UTC; duracao is therefore null. The Status Pages section was added on 27/10/25 after the original report. The page ends with a byline and a 'View more from Pete' link.
